title: Irish player ratings v Argentina: Hugo Keenan impresses in hat-trick display - The Irish Times
content: Ran an intelligent support line for his first, brilliant footwork for his second, a run-in for his third, aerially competitive, chased, harried and tackled, while covering the backfield with an impressive vigilance. Rating: 9 It was his arcing break that led to Ireland’s first try and he looked lethal in possession. Pace kills. Won some aerial duels too in an excellent all-round effort. His work in defence is occasionally overlooked but it should not be the case. Rating: 8 Unfussy and diligent in his work-rate he carried when his team needed and in defence was disciplined in jockeying at times and not biting in on the tackle. One or two nicely timed passes. Rating: 7 A couple of passes that were a little shy on the trajectory and pace, but he occupied the Pumas midfield and did carry well on occasion requiring more than one defender to stop him. A quieter outing by his lofty standards. Rating: 6 Given his absence from Test rugby through injury there was always going to be an acclimatisation process. Conceded an early penalty and snatched at a kick but his work for the first try and ability to occupy tacklers provided space for others was super. Grew into the game. Rating: 7 Bright opening, nice wrap on Ireland’s first try, kicked away a bit of ball, decisions he might like to have over again, but had numerous touches of class in both kicking and distribution. His try was a delight. Took the licks to let team-mates prosper. Rating: 8 Caught on cross-kick defending in the wide channel for Mateo Carreras try having twice called for backup. Sharp and alive in his work, his kicking was excellent, in a fine display. Rating: 8 Won a scrum penalty, carried through tacklers that gave his team front-foot ball and also occupied multiple defenders, intelligently looking for the pace between them. Nice mix to his work and got a late cameo at tighthead. Rating: 7 Involved multiple times for his try, throw, carry and pass, and then the act of dotting down. Superb in the loose, beating tackles with footwork and power before failing to return from a Head Injury Assessment. Rating: 7 Superb penalty turnover when Ireland were under serious pressure near their own line, he was another whose no nonsense carrying gave his team go-forward ball and made his tackles. Scrum went well too. Rating: 7 Good carry through traffic, his footwork into contact and lines of running was first class, while he was also a one-man maul wrecking machine. Another high-quality display. Rating: 8 Elected to carry when possession was slow and was typically difficult to shift when slowing down Argentina ruck ball and filching the odd one. Rating: 8 Beaten on the outside with a fend on a Pumas counterattack but thereafter his quality in the lineout caused Argentina huge problems, from pinching the ball outright to forcing crooked throws. Good overhead pass for Keenan hat-trick. Rating: 7 His clever feet for Sheehan’s try was a classic example of what he brings in the carrying game, so too his tackling when snuffing out visiting attacks. Rating: 7 Straight and hard in his running, took his lumps in two-man tackles without dialling down his commitment to the cause. Limped off early in the second half. Rating: 6 Rónan Kelleher was a first-half replacement and try scorer. Ciarán Frawley was lively. There were one or two other decent individual moments for those that came on but without quite making the anticipated impact. There’s an argument that the Argentina bench provided a little more impetus. Rating: 6 Andy Farrell will be pleased with the result, large tranches of the performance for a first outing since the summer and with the cohesion shown for the most part. His faith in rewarding a few players was repaid. Rating: 7 Join our dedicated Rugby WhatsApp channel for all the action What’s making headlines in the rugby world? title: Texas v Musk: how southern state Democrats won against the billionaire – explainer - The Guardian
content: Democrat James Talarico won a Senate seat in Texas, breaking a 38-year drought for his party in the Republican stronghold and delivering a stunning blow to Donald Trump. The race became one of the most expensive Senate contests in US history, with advertising spending topping $500m, according to estimates. GOP-aligned groups poured hundreds of millions of dollars into efforts to elect Ken Paxton, including substantial funding linked to multibillionaire Elon Musk, whom Talarico accused of trying to buy a Senate seat. title: Hamilton v Leclerc: how can Ferrari solve problem of two number one drivers? - The Guardian
content: The Scuderia are hopeful of being in the world championship mix next season but risk puncturing their chances if they can’t corral their men in the cockpits Going into this weekend’s São Paulo Grand Prix, all indications are that the status quo at Ferrari will no longer suffice for Lewis Hamilton if the Scuderia’s ambition to return their first drivers’ Formula One championship since 2007 is to be taken seriously. This year’s drivers’ title is already decided with Kimi Antonelli triumphant at the last round in Mexico and Ferrari are looking towards next season where they are hopeful of genuinely being in the mix against the Italian and Mercedes. However, after Hamilton and his teammate Charles Leclerc clashed at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez, the Briton clearly believes that a title tilt in 2027 might be at risk, as the team apparently vacillate on how to manage having two No 1 drivers, both determined to be the top dog around which Ferrari should coalesce. In Mexico, with Leclerc attempting to pass Hamilton, the move cost them both, Leclerc with a penalty and Hamilton in going wide and being passed by Max Verstappen who went on to win. The outcome denied Ferrari what would have been a likely victory and potentially a one-two. The team principal, Fred Vasseur, condemned the incident as demonstrating a lack of respect for the team and was expected to hold a crunch meeting with them both at Interlagos on Friday. It was not the first time this season the two Ferrari drivers have been uncompromising with one another. At Zandvoort Hamilton was frustrated when, on a different tyre strategy, Leclerc did not pit when first instructed to do so by the team in order to let the British driver past. A race later at Monza, Hamilton went down the inside of Leclerc into the first chicane and was squeezed wide by his teammate into the gravel. The notable difference after Mexico was Hamilton’s reaction. Previously he has been politic in stating they would deal with incidents behind closed doors – “offline” as he refers to it. After Mexico he publicly criticised Leclerc and before the race in Brazil was more bullish, refusing to be silenced in his criticism and making his position clear. “Naturally it’s not so easy having someone like me come into a team because I’m very outspoken,” he said. “I push and push and push for so many changes and I’m going to be pushing for more and as long as I’m here that’s how it’s going to be. I’m here to win.” That he is talking about it publicly indicates the seriousness of the situation. The team have no formal rules of engagement between the two and pointedly neither is considered the top driver in the way that Verstappen is at Red Bull. Last year with the team struggling it was irrelevant. This year the problem has been brought sharply into focus. With a title at stake in the future it could be the difference between winning and losing but this is far from a straightforward situation. Hamilton came to Ferrari on the back of enjoying de facto No 1 status at Mercedes, pretty much since Nico Rosberg retired after thein 2016 season. Leclerc, who is no less competitive, has enjoyed similar pre-eminence at Ferrari, with whom he has forged a strong relationship since he joined in 2019 and was long the favoured choice as their expected next champion. The complex demands and the fallout from letting them battle for dominance is far from new, as seen with Ayrton Senna and Alain Prost and Nigel Mansell and Nelson Piquet. Hamilton also knows about it, not least after his acrimonious fight with Rosberg in 2016. The latter was such that Mercedes, having been at pains to allow their drivers to race, had to impose rules of engagement. Vasseur has been painstaking so far in avoiding that scenario but he was left enormously frustrated after the incident in Mexico and knows how costly it could be. His is a very delicate balancing act however. McLaren had a similar problem with Oscar Piastri and Lando Norris in 2024 and 2025, and their efforts to allow their drivers to race without favour but also in managing them to the team’s advantage led to the adoption of their torturously complex “papaya rules”. These were satisfying to neither drivers nor fans, and did not appear particularly edifying to the team themselves. Notably however they did come out of it with the constructors’ title in 2024 and the double in 2025, a result that will not be lost on Ferrari. It has largely not been a problem for McLaren this season, with Norris enjoying a distinct advantage over his Australian teammate, of which Hamilton and Leclerc are aware. Both are determined to make themselves the focal point of the team; both are aware how important that is if the title is at stake. This has led to another fundamental problem for Ferrari. By not intervening in the process, they have seen the trust between the pair seemingly stretched to breaking point. Perhaps, it feels, within a whisker of becoming actively counterproductive from which a further, more damaging deterioration threatens. As Hamilton appears to be now insisting, Ferrari must address the issue but Leclerc cannot be faulted for simply following his instincts as a competitor. Both drivers are committed to the team but both are as equally determined to win, ambitions that match those of the Scuderia, which if they are to be met they must surely now look to manage. In first practice at Interlagos, McLaren’s Norris topped the timesheets in front of the new champion Antonelli in second, with Verstappen third and Hamilton fourth. In the afternoon Antonelli was on top, from Norris and Verstappen with Mercedes’ George Russell in fourth. Russell is, however, set to take a five-place grid penalty on Sunday for using a new engine in Brazil. Hamilton and Leclerc were in sixth and seventh. title: Canandaigua vs. Greece Athena score, updates from Section V football title game - Yahoo Sports
content: Canandaigua confirmed what many speculated all season. A gap existed between these Gray Wolves and the rest of Section V's Class A2 football teams. They proved it Nov. 6 in a championship rout. No. 1 Canandaigua (9-1) defeated No. 7 Greece Athena (4-6), 35-6, in the Class A2 final at Gates Chili High School. Aleks Hawyrschuk scored four rushing touchdowns and Brandon Dowitsch made two interceptions as the Wolves erased Athena's passing attack. That ended the Trojans' improbable playoff run and sealed the 12th sectional title in Canandaigua's rich football history. "We thought that, if could control the line of scrimmage and possess the ball, we could control the game," Canandaigua coach Jeff Welch said. "(Hawrsychuk) had some really good runs but our line controlled the game." Hawryschuk finished with 36 carries for 206 yards and four TDs. Look back at game action below. Canandaigua defeated Greece Athena, 35-6, to win the 2026 Section V Class A2 football championship. Aleks Hawryschuk scored four rushing touchdowns, Brandon Dowitsch made two interceptions, and Declan Cooney returned an interception for a touchdown in the win. Canandaigua quickly answered Athena's touchdown run. Aleks Hawrsychuk ran for his fourth touchdown of the night after the Gray Wolves recovered an onside kick attempt. They lead, 35-6, with 5:23 left in the fourth quarter. Travis Portis ran for an Athena touchdown with 6:14 left in the game. Nice offensive answer by the Trojans after Canandaigua stretched its lead to four scores. Canandaigua leads, 28-6, midway through the fourth quarter. Aleks Hawryschuk scored his third touchdown for Canandaigua on an 11-yard run with 11:11 remaining in the fourth quarter. Athena punted for the second time this half before the Gray Wolves' scoring drive. Pass defense has keyed the Canandaigua defense. Gray Wolves have several pass break-ups in addition to their two interceptions. Athena and Canandaigua traded third-quarter punts on each side's initial drive. Canandaigua leads, 21-0, with 1:39 left in the third. A pair of rushing touchdowns by Aleks Hawryschuk bookended a pick six by Declan Cooney. Canandaigua scored on two of its four possessions in the first half. Canandaigua's offense has consisted of a steady diet of runs. Hawryschuk, Isaac Dolph and Landon Mortimer have toted most of the carries. Aleks Hawrsychuk scored his second rushing touchdown of the evening with roughly three minutes remaining in the second quarter. Brandon Dowitsch ended Athena's second drive with an interception for Canandaigua. Athena, however, turned the Gray Wolves over on downs in the red zone. Two plays later, Declan Cooney grabbed an interception for Canandaigua and returned it for a touchdown. CA leads, 14-0, with 6:56 left in the second quarter after a 2-point conversion run by Brady Davern. Athena blocked the extra point attempt following Canandaigua's first touchdown. Aleks Hawryschuk scored the game's first touchdown for Canandaigua with 11:49 left in the second quarter, capping a long drive which proved much more successful than the Gray Wolves' first. Greece Athena's opening drive brought the Trojans to the Canandaigua 8-yard line before a turnover on downs. Scoreless with 3:40 remaining in the first quarter. Canandaigua opened the A2 final with a three-and-out on its first offensive possession. Sophomore Brady Davern made his third consecutive start at quarterback. Path to final: Defeated No. 2 Brockport (49-35), No. 6 Irondequoit (43-41) Path to final: Defeated No. 8 Greece Olympia-Odyssey (49-13), No. 4 Vertus (34-0) Canandaigua and Greece Athena are scheduled for a 5 p.m. kickoff in the Section V Class A2 football championship game. Gates Chili High School, located at 1 Spartan Way, will host the Section V Class A2 football championship game. title: We Took a Cadillac XLR-V Onto Europe’s Most Challenging Roads, and It Delivered - MotorTrend
content: We tackled some of Europe’s fastest and most challenging roads in a Cadillac. [This story originally appeared in the January 2008 issue of Motor Trend with the headline "A Long Way From Motown," and comes from a time when we had a space in our name.] The Porsches don’t want to play. Over 1000 hard-charging miles in two days across Germany, Austria, and Italy, and not one appears in the Cadillac’s sights. Which is a pity, because our wedgy, quad-piped XLR-V is locked and loaded for 911s. Whoa! Back up a minute! Did I just say we went chasing Porsches … in a Cadillac? In Germany? Um, yeah. Because that’s exactly what we did. And while the 911s proved elusive, no one—apart from a lunatic in a black BMW 645i convertible who kept the hammer down in a speed-limited construction zone—passed our XLR-V on the autobahnen. Not the silver-haired guy in the big, black Audi S8 with Wuppertal plates. Nor the guy in the E46 M3 who tried to run with us near Nuremberg. Nor even the guy in the AMG Benz who gave us a cold, hard stare after we blew by him near Mainz. They couldn’t keep up. Cadillac general manager Jim Taylor clearly has a sense of adventure, because when I idly suggested a while back it might be fun to disable the 155-mph speed limiter on an XLR-V and take it to Germany to see what it would do on highways with no speed limits, he didn’t suddenly look at his watch and start mumbling something about a meeting he had to catch. Instead, he simply cracked a wry grin: “That sounds like fun. Let me see what I can do.” Third gear is stunning, giving you an effective operating range of 37 to 129 mph. Lord only knows what it took to shepherd the idea through GM; every few months I’d see Taylor at some event or other and he’d always say, “I haven’t forgotten.” But Cadillac’s decision to hold preview drives of the all-new CTS sedan at the Nürburgring made a bunch of logistics a whole lot easier, which is how photographer Mark Bramley and I came to be pulling out of the car park of the Hyatt Regency Hotel in Mainz, Germany, bound for Italy and the famed Stelvio Pass in an Infrared metallic XLR-V. Why the Stelvio Pass? Well, as British mountaineer George Leigh Mallory explained when asked in 1923 why he wanted to climb Mt. Everest: “Because it’s there.” Located where Switzerland kisses Italy and Austria, the 9045-foot Stelvio is the second-highest paved pass in the Alps. Originally built in the 1820s, and little changed since, it reaches a one-in-nine gradient at some points and features 48 hairpins on the northern side. The view of the road writhing down the ancient glacial valley is one of the most iconic in motoring. “Our” XLR-V was stock apart from a simple change to the engine-management computer that banished the speed nanny to the electronic ether. GM also took the precaution of X-raying the wheels and tires for any cracks or faults, though if you think about it, you’re not going to be in that much more trouble if a tire pops at 170 mph or so than if it does at the regulation 155. Still, it’s nice to know they care. Contrary to popular legend, Germany’s autobahnen aren’t pedal-to-the-metal paradises where you can run as fast as you dare, as long as you like. Germany is slightly smaller than Montana, but has a population of more than 80 million people. So many of the country’s superhighways often look like rush hour in L.A., clogged with slow-moving cars and trucks. The natural gait of the XLR-V is somewhere between 135 and 140 mph. We take the long way out of Mainz to avoid the worst of the congestion, driving west, then south, before swinging east to cross the Rhine and head toward Heidelberg. Just as we turn east, where the A61 meets the A6, we bust the second autobahn myth: There are speed limits, and they’re ruthlessly enforced. Wheeling around a long on-ramp, something flashes in my peripheral vision, and as we clear the corner there’s a German police car, blue lights flashing along with a “Follow Me” sign—helpfully in English and French, as well as in German. He leads us into a nearby rest area where we join an orderly line of fellow drivers, licenses and wallets in hand, standing outside a Mercedes van. A guardrail-mounted speed camera has nailed the XLR-V at 80 mph in a 60 zone. As we wait, Bramley says Germany’s started to crack down hard on speeding drivers and warns me this could be expensive. As it turns out, there’s a sliding scale of fines, and foreigners get off a lot more lightly than do Germans. The cop relieves me of 95 euro—about $130. “For you, it’s cheap,” he smiles. Transaction over, we walk back to the car. I’m just about to fire up the supercharged V-8 when I see the cop striding toward us. Uh-oh, here comes the lecture. I roll down the window. The cop reaches into his pocket, pulls out a packet of cigarettes, and eyes the Michigan-plated Caddy, the brash Yank on a European vacation. Suddenly, he grins: “Now, I must say this: Gentlemen, start your engines!” Then he throws back his head, and roars with laughter. A German traffic cop with a sense of humor. Now I’ve seen everything. Back on the road, and clear of speed limits, we loaf along at 100 mph or so until the traffic clears and I can nail the gas. There’s a momentary lull as the six-speed auto shuffles back a couple ratios, then the Northstar growls into action. I see 168 mph on the head-up display (the speedo runs only to 160) before the traffic builds again, and I’m forced to back off. Analog speedo tops out at 160 mph, but we saw 171 mph on the head-up digital display. We cruise as fast as the traffic allows down to the Austrian border. The XLR-V’s natural gait is somewhere between 135 and 140 mph—a relatively restrained 2800 to 3000 rpm in the moonshot sixth gear. At these speeds it feels as comfortable, relaxed, and stable as an SL, though there’s much more wind noise from around the roof than in the Mercedes. Bramley no stranger to fast and exotic European machinery, raises an approving eyebrow. “It’s better than I thought it would be,” he says. The Cadillac is far from a Benz rival in other ways, though—you need only one glance around the cabin, taking in the cheap-looking plastics, old-school switchgear, and low-rent graphics to see that. The ergonomics could be better, too: The seat cushion is too short, and the pedals too high and vertical. You’d never guess GM once led the world in the study of biomechanics. It’s late afternoon by the time we reach Italy and the north side of the Stelvio. The XLR-V has proven surprisingly quick and agile on the smooth mountain roads, reminding me a lot—and, yes, I’m surprised to find myself writing this—of our Jaguar XKR long-termer. The Cadillac has that same fast yet relaxed feel of the Jag, although the British car steers more crisply, rides better, brakes harder, and feels much more rigidly constructed. Still, there’s the genesis of a great GT in this Cadillac. All GM has to do is sweat the details. The 443-horsepower, supercharged Northstar V-8 is a gem, smooth and flexible and willing to rev, with a solid side order of torque on hand whenever you need it. I move the shift lever across the gate into manual mode, working through second, third, and fourth as we zigzag through the hills. Third gear is stunning—the V-8 pulls like a train from 2000 rpm and doesn’t stop until it nudges 6700, giving you an effective operating range of 37 to 129 mph. The Caddy demolishes short straightaways and barely draws breath up the hills, the V-8 exhaust note booming off the rock walls. The Stelvio itself is astonishing. The road climbs steadily through the forest, switchbacks here and there, before we break through the treeline. Then the hairpins pile one on top of the other; in places the road doubles back on itself two or three times in the space of a few hundred yards. Traffic’s light—most of the bikers who swarm over the place on summer weekends are already in their hotels enjoying an early evening beer—so I can push a little, punching hard out of the hairpins in first gear, snick-snicking into second, then third, before getting hard on the brakes, and double-pumping the shift lever to grab first again for another hairpin. Even with power steering and no clutch pedal, climbing the Stelvio is a physical business. We check into one of the hotels at the very top of the pass. Just down the hill, on the southern side, is the Swiss border. We drive down and cross over, just for the hell of it: It’s not often you get to drive through four countries in one day. Especially in a Cadillac. The next morning dawns bright and clear, so we’re up before breakfast, working the photo ops on the north side of the pass. By the time we finish, it’s past 9 a.m., and Bramley’s due on a 6 p.m. plane out of Frankfurt, more than 500 miles away. I look at the maps and decide we’ll cut east to pick up the autostrada at Merano and drive south to join the A22, which will take us up and over the Brenner Pass back into Austria. It’s going to be a hard slog. The XLR-V draws lots of stares from the car-savvy Italians as we stalk through the shoals of Fiats and Fords on the Brenner Pass. Cadillac’s distinctive visual signature—confident, powerful, chiseled—stands out among the Euro-chic background noise. As with the mechanical package, there’s a world-beating car lurking here, but GM needs to improve panel fit and paint finish (I’ve seen runs along the edge of an XLR-V hood) and finesse the jewelry. The traffic’s heavy, but flowing briskly, and the run down from the top of the Brenner Pass toward Innsbruck gives us the best gas mileage of the trip, 20.5 mpg at an average of 61 mph. But our hopes of making good time to Frankfurt are dashed by a traffic jam just inside the German border, south of Munich. I check the sat nav to find a back road off the autobahn at the next exit, but by the time we wind through a host of picturesque villages and get back onto the A8, we’ve probably burned an hour. We skirt around the east side of Munich and head north, back toward Nuremberg. The traffic clears, and we can run 125-130 mph for a bit. But only a bit—one minute the trip computer says we have 40 miles’ worth of gas left, next we’re running on fumes. I soft-pedal it into a gas station near Nuremberg and pump 15.8 gallons into the tank. We’re struggling to get much more than 250 miles between fuel stops. Memo, Cadillac: A 20-gallon tank would be nice. We make Frankfurt just in time, and I head back to Mainz after dropping Bramley at Departures, looping around to get to a quiet autobahn on the other side of the city. I’m still looking for Porsches. And room to top 168 mph. The A63 is near empty, and unrestricted. Perfect. I settle back in the seat and nail the gas. The Northstar growls, the induction roar ratcheting up an octave as the tach needle swings past 3600 rpm. First gear runs to 47 mph, second to 80, third 124, and fourth hits 165. The transmission slips into fifth, and the digital display keeps ticking off the increments, more slowly now. 169…170…171 mph. And that’s it, not the least because I’ve just chewed through a quarter tank of gas in less than 15 minutes, and I have to find a gas station again. Okay, I didn’t get to surprise any 911s. But I did learn one thing: There’s no reason why Cadillac can’t build a world-beating GT. The XLR-V’s far from perfect, but it’s a lot more at home in Europe than you might think. title: Since the 1987 title game defeat, Syracuse basketball is undefeated v. Indiana - Sports Illustrated
content: Sorry, Orange Nation. We well know the picture above will always hurt, albeit a big part of the sting was eased with the 2003 national championship in the same building. We were sitting courtside just to the right of the Indiana bench in the then-Louisiana Superdome on the evening of Monday, March 30, 1987, anchoring our statewide radio network broadcast of the '87 Final Four. With SU up 73-72 with 28 seconds left and Derrick Coleman headed to the foul line for a 1-and-1 opportunity, we distinctly remember sharing glances and a "maybe SU is going to win the title" look with the late program booster and close Jim Boeheim friend Bill Rapp, who kept the official Syracuse scorebook for games in that era. But it was not to be. Alas, after Coleman missed the front end, and with SU defenders back on defense, the Hoosiers raced down to set up the final sequence and we all know that Keith Smart's shot took care of matters with four seconds left, as Hall of Famer Bob Knight defeated Hall of Famer Boeheim. Beginning two seasons later and right up until the 2021-22 campaign, there have been six SU wins over IU coming in distinctly different fashions in the six games played, from blowouts to double overtime, but always a 'Cuse win, almost like its own curse set on the Hoosiers program. Monday night at Gainbridge Fieldhouse (6:30 p.m. ET / FS1), it will be a tall task for the Orange (2-0) with a rebuilt roster playing its third game together, against the Hoosiers (2-0) who received votes in this week's Top 25 polls. It is a made-for-TV, non-conference matchup that fits Gerry McNamara's vision of an early season mix of winnable games at home, and challenging contests on the road. Here is a capsule look back on the six Syracuse Indiana games played since the 1987 title game defeat: 1988 - This game will forever be remembered for the Sherman Douglas' hike-between-his-legs pass to Stevie Thompson for a dunk that wowed the crowd on route to a 102-78 rout. 1990 - In a game ending in the early monring hours eastern time, the Orangmen held off IU in Maui 77-74 behind 28 points from Billy Owens. 1998 - The 'Cuse again won the Maui title over Indiana by pulling past the Hoosiers in the second half of a 76-63 victory. Five SU players hit double figures, including Jason Hart with 17 points. 2013 - One of the most unsung, late blooming Boeheim teams (a fourth seed) compleley flummoxed top-seed Indiana with its 2-3 zone in an NCAA Sweet 16 game in Washington, winning 61-50. Michael Carter-Williams had 24 of the team's 61 points. 2013 - Ranked 4th nationally, SU had a big second half 25-4 run to blow open its ACC/Big Ten Challenge game with IU in the Dome. Trevor Cooney had 12 of his team-high 21 points during the second half run to lead SU to the 69-52 victory. 2021 - In a wild, double overtime affair in the Dome, Boeheim's final game coaching against Indiana resulted in a 112-110 win, when Joe Girard raced downcourt and was fouled shooting, and hit two free throws to clinch the win. title: How to sink a boat: Prepping CFCC's R/V Cape Hatteras for its next chapter - WHQR
content: Sinking a boat is an elaborate undertaking, according to Jordan Byrum, the Enhancement Project Manager for the North Carolina Division of Marine Fisheries. The agency runs an artificial reef program, which turns retired boats, recycled concrete pipe, and chunks of decommissioned bridges into habitat features for wildlife and divers. “North Carolina has managed an artificial reef program since the 1970s,” he told WHQR. “Prior to that, it was a little bit of the wild west, with people dropping refrigerators and cars and Lord knows what.” The state formalized the program and started sinking derelict World War II vessels up and down the coast. In just a few months, the Cape Hatteras, a 135-foot boat that served as a ‘floating classroom’ for students at Cape Fear Community College, will join other retired vessels in about 80 feet of water, 18 miles off of Wrightsville Beach. First, the boat will undergo a deep cleaning. Anything that could contaminate the water or float away will be removed. Byrum described the process. “As far as sinking goes, a lot of access holes get cut anyway,” he elaborated. “They also help vent air whenever the vessel gets sunk. So they'll probably install a valve or a series of valves in the bottom of the vessel, and so when we get on site and it gets anchored in the correct spot, one of the contractors will go and open those valves. The access holes, which were cut to remove the engine and other components, will allow water to rush in and sink the boat. There’s no exact date for the sinking yet. Byrum says divers and researchers visiting the site can expect to see gag grouper, black sea bass, amberjacks, sharks, and American red snapper. As for CFCC's marine technology program, it's getting a new 86-foot catamaran, currently under construction and expected to arrive this winter, according to CFCC.

title: Nottingham Forest v Man City: Key stats and talking points - Yahoo Sports
content: "If you lose four of the last five games, it's not good enough. And that's why, for me, it's now time that we change things, that I change things, and that's what I will do." So said Nottingham Forest head coach Oliver Glasner after seeing his side lose at Brentford last weekend, despite having twice as many shots as their opponents (15 to seven) and three times as many attempts from inside the penalty area (nine to three). For the seventh time in nine matches in this Premier League campaign, Forest outperformed the opposing team in terms of xG, yet they have turned that dominant stat into just one win and six points in total. Forest, who have yet to score at home in any competition this season, have scored just six Premier League goals from an xG total of 14.34, an under-performance of 8.34 goals. That's comfortably the worst differential of any team this season, and the biggest under-performance by a side after nine Premier League games since at least 2021-22, when Opta introduced its revamped xG model. It is the problem Glasner has to solve – the Austrian, who is the fifth man to take charge of Forest since the start of last season, is confident of doing so but is well aware that if he can't, owner Evangelos Marinakis may well once again act sooner rather than later. "I will tell what we want to do, what we have to do," said Glasner. "And if the players buy in, I think we can have a turnaround. And if not, the sixth manager will come in." Manchester City got back to winning ways in Europe in midweek after a three-game spell that included two league defeats and needing penalties to get past Brighton in the Carabao Cup. With Arsenal taking full advantage of City's stutter, Enzo Maresca's side will need to start putting aside their recent unconvincing form, especially with a league game against the champions looming at the end of the month. City are comfortably outscoring Arsenal but they have conceded twice as many goals as the Gunners in the Premier League, while they have looked vulnerable defensively. They haven't kept a clean sheet in their past seven matches, conceding 14 times, and have suffered several high-profile lapses at the back. "We are creating many chances in each game but we need to avoid silly goals," said Maresca after City's victory in midweek, in which Gianluigi Donnarumma was caught out at his near post, one of several errors the Italian keeper has made this season. "At the moment, I'm not thinking about the goalkeeping situation," added Maresca, who insists Donnarumma's form "is not a concern".

title: Xavier v. Eastern Michigan: Preview - Yahoo Sports
content: Xavier romped to a win over Mount St. Mary's on opening night, but the test seems like it will be much sterner in their second outing of the season. Eastern Michigan comes in at 1-0 as well, having fended off Coastal Carolina, and hopes to make waves in the MAC this season after being picked 9th in the 12 team conference. The Eagles are in year one under Billy Donlon, who was formerly the head coach at Wright State and UMKC alongside assistant gigs at UNC Wilmington, Michigan, Northwestern, and most recently Clemson for the past four seasons. On offense, his teams tend to shoot the three decently well most of the time, but if they miss they're usually pretty content to leave it at that, with his teams' best offensive rebounding finish in 9 previous seasons being 293rd. After his first season at Wright State, he's never had a particularly good offense, having failed to crack the top 225 in his other 8 seasons as a head coach. Defense is another story, with Donlon's teams having a couple of standout attributes that have made his defenses some of the best in the low majors in his career. First of all, his teams are going to come after the ball. His defense ranked top 50 in turnover rate nationally in 5 of his 6 seasons at Wright State including a run of 13th, 4th, 15th, and 6th from 2011-2014. His UMKC teams were 52nd, 21st, and 37th in that category and were the bet defensive unit in the Summit in his final two seasons there. His teams also tend to rebound the ball well at that end, with 5 of his 9 seasons resulting in top 100 finishes in defensive rebound rate. The achilles heel for Donlon's defenses is twofold. Firstly, they send their opponents to the line an absurd amount, never even cracking the top 250 in defensive free throw rate. If you think the opponents need that reprieve from seeing their shots miss, you're wrong because 6 of Donlon's 9 teams have surrendered a 2 point field goal percentage above 50. Basically, if you can keep the ball long enough to shoot, you'll probably make it and if you miss it's probably because you were fouled. The name to know here is Mohammad Habhab, who was selected First Team All-MAC and dropped 34 and 13 on 7-16/2-3/18-21 shooting in the season opener. He averaged 14.2/8.3/3.1 last season as a Redshirt Freshman and elected to stay close to home for his second year, but will probably have opportunities in the portal to greatly enrich himself if he wants them. Junior guard Jabari Fitzpatrick was quiet in the opener, but is coming off a year where he averaged 15.0/4.5/2.6 at New Haven and dropped 29 and 32 points on Stonehill and Farleigh-Dickinson in back to back February outings. William & Mary transfer Killian Brockhoff was all but anonymous in the opener, posting just a rebound and a turnover in 16 minutes, but was a solid contributor for the Tribe last season. NJCAA Division II Player of the Year and National Champion Jaiden Martin was spectacular in the opener with 17 points and 3 steals on 6-11 shooting in his DI debut and will be hoping to follow that up in his first crack at a high major. 6'11" NAIA journeyman Kaden Johnson is tasked with covering the glass, which he did fairly well in the season opener, finishing with 8 points and 5 rebounds, all of which were defensive. The one player on the roster with high major experience is guard Braelon Green, who started his career at Arizona State before bouncing to Bowling Green and finally landing in Ypsilanti last year and averaging 4.6/1.8/1.4 and shooting a respectable 36% from three. Former UC Bearcat Sencire Harris transferred to EMU this spring, but quit the team a week ago to pursue (likely nonexistent) professional basketball opportunities, leaving the Eagles rotation a bit short. Take care of the ball– Donlon's teams are known for hounding the ball and are typically pretty unsuccessful on defense if they can't force turnovers. One gripe you could have about Xavier's overall performance on Monday is that they were sloppy with the ball. X has to clean that up to keep this one from getting interesting. Take advantage of the freebie battle– Again, speaking from history Donlon's teams aren't going to generate many second chances and they are going to opponents at the free throw line. The other major gripe about Xavier's opening game is that they shot 16-26 from the free throw line, which is bad. EMU only got back 8 misses against Coastal Carolina, so there isn't a reason to think that Xavier should struggle to keep them off the glass, but making ending possessions after one shot and converting at the line points of emphasis will take advantage of the things the opponent is worst at. Keep the pace high– Xavier's opening game featured 80 possessions, which played into their hands due to their roster construction and depth. EMU focuses on their all conference big man and is down a guard they though would be carrying a lot of the load in their rotation so the more like a track meet Xavier can make this, the better off they'll likely be.

title: 2 Colts defensive starters out v. Cowboys with injuries - Colts Wire
content: Indianapolis Colts' head coach Shane Steichen has ruled out two starters for Sunday's game against Dallas. LB Akeem Davis-Gaither (knee) and CB Justin Walley (knee) will both be sidelined. Neither player practiced this week as they work through their respective injuries. Walley did not play against Jacksonville. In his place, Kenneth Harris and Kapena Gushiken each saw slot snaps. Without Davis-Gaither, we should see rookie CJ Allen wear the green dot. He made his first start last week. Jaylon Carlies and Bryce Boettcher are candidates to start at the WILL linebacker position. Elsewhere, OT Jalen Travis (thumb/hamstring) and S AJ Haulcy (ankle) are both questionable. Haulcy was added to the injury report on Friday. Travis had been listed with a thumb injury the first two days; the hamstring injury was added on Friday. He was a full participant all three days. title: Sutton's predictions: Leeds v Tottenham - Yahoo Sports
content: Tottenham always seem to do well against Leeds United - they have only lost one of their past 15 meetings in the Premier League, going back almost 25 years. I am a little bit of a believer that some teams always do well, or badly, against certain opposition or on certain grounds. I had the same as a player when I had bogey teams or stadiums, as well as lucky ones. For example, while I always used to score against Everton at Goodison Park, I always had a stinker at Highfield Road, Coventry's old home, despite getting plenty of goals against them in home games for Blackburn. So, I am definitely not going for Leeds to win this - but do I back Tottenham to win again and continue their good run? Roberto de Zerbi's side have rocketed up the table on the back of three wins in a row, although they were helped out a lot by Jean-Philippe Mateta's red card in their victory over Crystal Palace last time out. Tottenham are flying at the moment, and their confidence is up - we are seeing a bit of a Spurs swagger for the first time in a long while. So, while I don't think they will make it four wins in a row, I don't see them being beaten, either. It's likely to be a very tight game. Leeds were a bit unlucky to lose to Bournemouth last week, but their lack of goals is becoming an issue.

title: ACC QB Handoff: Stanford’s Warren Tapped as Next House Class Rep - Sportico.com
content: The ACC-to-ACC quarterback pipeline is extending beyond the football field and into the courtroom. Stanford starting quarterback Davis Warren is poised to become the newest class representative of the House v. NCAA settlement, following in the footsteps of former Louisville QB Miller Moss. In a motion filed this week, attorneys representing the House class requested the court appoint Warren to the position, keeping an active ACC signal caller involved in overseeing the settlement’s 10-year injunctive relief. Warren, a sixth-year athlete, began his college playing career as a walk-on at Michigan, where he competed from 2021 to 2025 before transferring to Stanford this year. In a written declaration submitted to the court, Warren said he and Moss, who now plays with the Chicago Bears, have been friends “for many years” and that Moss was the one who suggested he take on the role. “I am interested in joining this litigation as a class representative because I believe it is the right thing to do,” Warren wrote. “I want to ensure that athletes’ voices are heard, that those in positions of power act in athletes’ best interests, and that athletes can make the most of their opportunities for compensation and benefits.” Warren’s prospective role creates an unusual legal dynamic in Stanford’s quarterback room: His teammate, senior Charlie Mirer, is actively challenging the authority of the enforcement body the House settlement created. In June, Mirer and USC freshman linebacker Talanoa Ili filed a class action lawsuit against the NCAA, the Power 4 conferences (including the ACC) and the College Sports Commission, contending that certain of the CSC’s restrictions on college athlete NIL rights violate statutes in California and 16 other states. Mirer and Ili argue that only federal legislation could supersede those state-level protections. They are asking a U.S. District Court judge to certify four classes of similarly situated athletes, appoint them as class representatives and award treble damages for the alleged antitrust violations. Importantly, the lawsuit does not challenge the House settlement itself, but the way it is being implemented. Mirer and Ili have a pending administrative motion to relate their litigation to House v. NCAA, which would place the new case before U.S. District Court Judge Claudia Wilken. Warren, for his part, said he has already “devoted significant time” to reviewing the settlement agreement along with the the pending appellate briefs field by objectors challenging the deal before the 9th Circuit. Warren disclosed he has received third-party NIL both as a walk-on and scholarship athlete and that his interest in serving as class representative is “not motivated by my personal gain.” On the field, Warren has thrown for 2,203 years this season for Stanford, which fell to 4-5 following last week’s loss to Louisville. Moss was added as a class representative in November 2025 after the original representatives—including Grant House, Tymir Oliver, Sedona Prince and DeWayne Carter—had exhausted their college eligibility. In approving the settlement, U.S. District Judge Claudia Wilken noted that while added new class representatives was not “necessary,” the agreement contemplated periodic appointments. Warren would become the second Stanford athlete to serve as class representative following former Cardinal soccer player Nya Harrison, who now plays for the NWSL’s San Diego Wave. title: Temporary Protected Status Abuse: Implications in a Post-Mullin v. Doe World - Columbia Political Review
content: Kristi Noem, former Secretary of Homeland Security, attempted to terminate 13 of the 17 existing Temporary Protected Status designations, leading to lengthy litigation on Secretary Noem’s procedural missteps. Photo Courtesy of Gage Skidmore. In 2011, Syria erupted into civil war between President Bashar Al-Assad’s authoritarian regime and a fractured opposition, taking over 580,000 lives while displacing more than 13 million Syrians between 2011 and 2024. In response, America designated “Temporary Protected Status,” or TPS, to Syria. Created in the Immigration Act of 1990, TPS is a temporary designation to countries that are deemed unsafe for nationals in the US to return to. The Secretary of Homeland Security grants these designations for reasons including war, natural disasters, and other extraordinary circumstances. TPS beneficiaries, after applying and passing a background check, can reside and work in the US, and cannot be removed during the designation period. Though TPS was intended to be temporary, many designations have lasted for decades. For example, Syria was designated TPS in 2012 and a series of extensions maintained the country's status for over a decade. As of March 2025, approximately 1.3 million individuals from 17 different countries benefited from TPS; however, following broader policies restricting immigration, the Trump administration has attempted to terminate 13 of the 17 TPS designations. In September of 2025, then-Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem terminated Syria’s designation, giving 60 days notice to the 6,100 Syrian TPS holders in the US that they could not legally remain in the country. A portion of these Syrians sued in the Southern District of New York in Doe v. Noem, arguing that the termination was arbitrary because required procedural steps weren’t followed. In late 2025, a US district court ruled that Secretary Noem likely violated the TPS statute by not adequately consulting appropriate agencies as required in Section 3a of 8 U.S. Code § 1254a:The Attorney General, after consultation with appropriate agencies of the Government, shall review the conditions in the foreign state. . .for which a designation is in effect. [...] and shall determine whether the conditions for such designation [...] continue to be met. Though the act does not list specific agencies that are deemed “appropriate”, past termination procedures have typically included the Department of State, the National Security Council, and occasionally the Department of Justice. These agencies can inform the Secretary about the conditions in countries designated for TPS and whether it would be advisable to terminate or redesignate TPS. The government appealed the district court’s decision to the US Supreme Court, where it was consolidated with a similar case challenging Haiti’s TPS termination (Miot v. Trump), and titled Mullin v. Doe, et al. On June 25th in a 6-3 decision, the Supreme Court upheld the termination of both Syria’s and Haiti’s TPS. This decision gives undue discretion over TPS designations to the executive branch and continues a trend of eroding the power of the judicial branch to provide constitutional checks on executive authority; furthermore, it allows for abuse of the TPS system, evidenced by the violation of Syria's TPS termination process and the country’s continually unsafe conditions. The primary question in Mullin v. Doe concerned the availability of judicial review of non-constitutional decisions made by DHS in a TPS termination. The Supreme Court ultimately barred itself from reviewing any TPS designations and terminations, including procedural steps that precede them. The decision hinged on the meaning of the word “determine.” As Justice Alito writes in the majority opinion, “The relevant provision bars judicial review of any determination of the [Secretary of Homeland Security] with respect to the designation, or termination or extension of a designation, of a foreign state.” Justice Alito, alongside the Court’s conservative majority, interprets “determine” as referring to the authority to make terminations, designations, and any related procedural steps taken—“procedural determinations.” Justice Elena Kagan dissented, asserting that “determine” more accurately refers to the final decisions (specifically, designations and terminations) and not the process. Indeed, Justice Alito’s interpretation of “determine” seems to undermine court precedent. In the 1991 case McNary v. Haitian Refugee Center, the Court held that statutory and constitutional challenges to procedures used by the Immigration and Naturalization Service (INS) to the Special Agricultural Worker program were reviewable. The Court drew a distinction between legal challenges to an individual decision and challenges to the process by which that decision was made. Mullin v. Doe establishes a new precedent that places TP procedural determinations beyond judicial review and leaves them to the Secretary of Homeland Security, leaving the TPS program vulnerable to political whims of the executive branch. Although only 6,000 Syrian nationals reside in the US under TPS, analyzing Syria’s termination process can expose the possible consequences of DHS’s procedural missteps. First, Secretary Noem did not take the necessary procedural steps required by the TPS statute to terminate Syria’s TPS. Her sole form of “consultation” with relevant agencies (as required by the statute) consisted of a single email to the State Department stating that Haiti and Syria were up for TPS review, to which the department responded that it had “no foreign policy concerns.” She did consult with the National Security Council or Department of Justice, and her communication with the State Department lacked any discussion of the country's conditions. Though she was caught, the termination was upheld because the Court deemed procedural determinations as unreviewable. Such failures of procedure will continue to be exempt from review, creating a harmful precedent that allows for abuse of TPS. This abuse could have far-reaching consequences, as a Secretary of Homeland Security could terminate a TPS designation for a country that remains unsafe. Syria can again be used as an example. DHS termination report on Syria’s TPS had its foundations in the 2024 overthrow of the Assad regime, which was followed by a transitional government under Ahmed Al-Sharaa. Though a termination report is a required part of the TPS termination process, the report’s justifications are flawed, perhaps due to a lack of consultation with government agencies. The report uses two main pieces of evidence to support the termination: First, DHS cites the 1.2 million Syrian refugees who’ve returned to the country after Assad’s overthrow; however, this return was primarily driven by “push” rather than “pull” factors. In Lebanon, where 1.3 million Syrian refugees reside, over 90%live in extreme poverty and face frequent deportations. In Turkey, which hosts 3.2 million Syrian refugees, 90% are unable to cover monthly expenses. Worse, Turkey has growing anti-Syrian refugee sentiment, and Human Rights Watch has documented many Syrians being coerced into signing “voluntary return” contracts. In the European Union, where 1.4 million Syrian refugees reside, many member states have suspended asylum processing and revoked protection status for Syrians. DHS’s use of refugee return statistics fails to account for clear evidence suggesting that the return of the refugees has little to do with conditions in Syria. The second justification made by DHS concerns decreasing violence, claiming that the sporadic nature of violence in Syria fails to pose a serious threat to returning Syrians. While violence in Syria doesn’t continue at the same severity as during the Civil War, it remains serious. Syria’s transitional government identifies as Sunni, but substantial Kurdish, Druze, and Alawite populations reside throughout the nation. In 2025, Al-Sharaa’s transitional government committed violent abuses against these minority populations, including sexual violence against Druze communities and identity-based killings of Alawites. Terminating TPS would put thousands more lives at risk, increasing minority displacement. Until the transitional government integrates minority communities into the government, safety is far from ensured for Syrians. DHS claims further undermine realities for both minority and majority Syrians. Almost 70%of the population requires humanitarian assistance, a heavily rationed electric system limits electricity, and over 80%of Syrian families cannot meet their food needs; furthermore, 15.4 million Syrians are at risk of injury or death due to unexploded ordnance. Ultimately, conditions in Syria are unsafe for Syrian TPS holders to return to. DHS’s disregard for such conditions shows how consequential an abuse of TPS terminations could be—abuse that was permitted by the U.S. Supreme Court. The termination of Syria’s TPS could impact the U.S. relationship with Syria. As Syria continues to transition under Ahmed Al-Sharaa’s government, the country could be an important situational ally of the U.S. in Middle Eastern conflicts. Though one could view terminating TPS as a sign of trust, forcefully deporting 6,100 Syrian nationals could increase pressure on the fledgling administration; furthermore, the termination would signify an American disinterest in intervening in the Middle East, a harmful narrative for U.S. efforts in the region. What would hypothetically follow Mullin v. Doe is frightening: countries still unsafe for nationals to return to could have their TPS designations terminated for domestic political reasons without procedural safeguards. In light of Syria’s unjustified TPS termination, it is plausible that the Trump administration’s other TPS terminations are similarly flawed. The consequences are drastic: up to 1.3 million people living and working in the U.S. for decades could be sent back to countries that remain unsafe and be put at risk of poverty and violence. One way to account for the harmful impact of Mullin v. Doe is for Congress to amend the TPS statute to specify that procedural determinations remain reviewable, followed by the establishment of a more concrete termination and designation procedure. For instance, this could include a mandated consultation with the State Department that includes preset questions directly addressing country conditions. This would allow for TPS abuse to be investigated and addressed in federal courts. On a broader level, the TPS system needs reform to include more comprehensive positive liberties. As designations have often lasted decades, the program has become less “temporary”; policymakers should consider providing TPS holders who have resided and worked in the U.S. for many years with a path to U.S. citizenship. Additionally, many countries granted TPS have been ravaged by war and natural disasters—provisions should be created to guarantee safe housing and food access for TPS holders in their home countries after a termination. TPS can be an effective way for the U.S. to provide humanitarian assistance to individuals from struggling countries, but these loopholes within the law leave the system vulnerable to unjustified terminations for the sake of political expediency. Until they are addressed, the potential for terrible injustice to TPS holders remains. Roshan Hoban (CC ‘30) is an incoming freshman studying Economics-Political Science.  He can be reached at rgh2137@columbia.edu.

title: Scotland v New Zealand prediction: All Blacks to 'navigate tricky assignment' and extend unbeaten streak against 'competitive' hosts - Planet Rugby
content: Sione Tuipulotu and Jordie Barrett image Scotland and New Zealand are set to resume their rivalry which dates back to 1905 when they meet in their eagerly anticipated Nations Championship Test at Murrayfield on Saturday. Despite having home ground advantage, Scotland head into this encounter as the underdogs after failing to beat the All Blacks in the 33 previous encounters between these countries. New Zealand have been victorious in 31 of those Tests while the best results in this fixture for the Scots were a couple of draws which they registered in 1964 and 1983. Although they are yet to secure a victory against the men in black, Gregor Townsend‘s troops head into this clash with some confidence as they currently occupy second position in the Nations Championship’s Northern Hemisphere standings, just one point adrift of France. This, after the Scots notched wins over Argentina and Fiji while also suffering a defeat against South Africa during the Southern Hemisphere leg of the competition in July. Meanwhile, the All Blacks started Dave Rennie‘s reign as head coach in style with impressive Nations Championship triumphs over France, Italy and Ireland and those results mean they are in second place in the tournament’s Southern Hemisphere table with South Africa sitting pretty in top spot by virtue of a superior points difference. Although there’s been plenty of misery for Scotland in this fixture over the years, they have been competitive against the All Blacks recently. Despite losing their last four Tests to the men in black, three of those defeats were by eight points while a fourth one – in 2017 – was by just five. Those results will give the Scots some hope of causing an upset this weekend. These are two teams who employ similar game-plans in which a free-flowing and expansive approach on attack is preferred but in order for the respective backlines to impress with ball in hand, the forward battle will be crucial in deciding the eventual outcome of this fixture. One of the major reasons for the All Blacks’ 3-1 series defeat against the Springboks was their inability to get the better of the world champions in the tight exchanges particularly their scrummaging and lineout efforts. The Boks put plenty of pressure on the All Blacks at scrum time and Rennie’s charges conceded 14 penalties as well as a penalty try from the set-piece over the four Tests between the arch rivals while South Africa also stole eight lineout balls during the series. While they are expected to improve in both those departments against Scotland, the home side showed during this year’s Six Nations and most of their previous Nations Championship Tests that their set-piece work has improved, particularly their scrummaging and that facet of play could prove crucial in the grander scheme of things. Whoever dominates up front and provides good front foot ball and speedy possession to their backline should emerge victorious. ﻿ Rennie is wary of the threat posed by Scotland particularly at Murrayfield where they usually impress in front of their home fans. “We’re aware we’re playing a Scottish side that’s very confident at home,” he said. “They’ll have a lot of belief, but we’ve got to back our game as well. “Our job is to put them under as much pressure as possible and take the crowd out of the game.” Meanwhile, Townsend is preparing his troops for a tough encounter but expects a different challenge from the men in black under Rennie’s guidance after he replaced Scott Robertson. “It’s great we now get this opportunity to play New Zealand again but it’s a different New Zealand team,” he said. “It’s a team that is playing much more ambitious rugby. “They’re informed, they’re cohesive. They played a lot of Test matches over the summer, so it might not be the same game that transpires.” Scotland team v All Blacks: British and Irish Lions duo return amid strong selection as Gregor Townsend seeks first-ever win over New Zealand Scotland have been boosted by the return of two of their backline stalwarts in experienced outside centre Huw Jones and full-back Blair Kinghorn, who are set to make their international comebacks after missing their country’s July internationals. Jones was sidelined due to a foot injury but has made a full recovery and lines up in midfield alongside Scotland skipper Sione Tuipulotu to resume their highly successful Huwipulotu partnership. Brilliant with ball in hand, Jones is renowned for running superb attacking lines and he will be expected to test the All Blacks’ defence once he builds up a head of steam. Meanwhile, Kinghorn was dropped from Scotland’s squad for their previous Nations Championship matches and is set to make his Test return via the bench after being named amongst the replacements for this fixture. A brilliant attacker, who is also solid under the high ball and in defence, he will be champing at the bit to make an impact in this match. If Scotland want to end their winless streak against New Zealand then their fly-half Finn Russell will have to produce one of his best performances. A superb playmaker, who has the ability to unlock the tightest defences with his superb skill-set and if he does that this weekend, the home side could emerge victorious. Amongst Scotland’s forwards, keep an eye on Jack Dempsey, who usually gets through plenty of work as a ball carrier but also puts his body on the line on defence where he is renowned for putting in some big hits. For New Zealand, experienced backline stars Damian McKenzie and Beauden Barrett showed in their recent Bledisloe Cup triumphs over Australia that they still have important roles to play in the international arena. Like those encounters, McKenzie starts at fly-half and Barrett at full-back and just like the clashes against the Wallabies, they are expected to provide a twin playmaking threat on attack. Amongst the forwards, stand-in skipper Codie Taylor might be in the twilight of his career but he showed against the Wallabies that he can still produce impressive performances at Test level. Apart from impressing as a player, Taylor has led his troops well, since replacing the injured Ardie Savea as captain, and his leadership skills will be crucial against the Scots. Another player whose stocks have risen recently is star loose forward Peter Lakai who was one of the All Blacks’ best players during their recent series against the Springboks. Capable of playing in all three back-row positions, the 23-year-old will play on the openside flank in this clash and he is sure to be in the thick of the action on either side of the ball. While there are several enticing direct duels lined up across the pitch, the midfield battle will be crucial particularly between the two inside centres, Scotland’s Sione Tuipulotu and New Zealand’s Jordie Barrett, who both possess excellent all-round skill-sets. Both are outstanding with ball in hand and will be determined to make an impact in that department. Tuipulotu is a powerful ball carrier who enjoys the direct route which usually gives his side good momentum. However, he also possesses deft touches and his superb distribution skills will be expected to create some try-scoring opportunities for his team-mates. However, his direct opponent Barrett comes into this clash in a rich vein of form as he has been at the forefront of New Zealand’s onslaught in the international arena in 2026. The 29-year-old started at inside centre in eight of his country’s nine Tests played this year and whether on defence or attack, he has been a vital cog in the All Blacks machine. After delivering several impressive performances against New Zealand recently, Scotland will be in a confident mood ahead of this match. However, the All Blacks have too much class across the park and although this will be a tricky assignment to navigate, their winless streak in this fixture will continue. title: Flanders Scientific FSI VP & V Series - Newsshooter
content: Flanders Scientific has introduced the FSI VP and V Series, which are touted to deliver the company’s renowned image quality at a more accessible price. The FSI VP and V Series consists of seven new QD-OLED HDR monitors featuring the same panels, color engine, and GaiaColor calibration tools as the company’s flagship XMP Series. The new monitors were designed for workflows that don’t require the XMP Series’ advanced onboard scopes, Look LUTs, or Livegrade integration. The VP Series features 12G-SDI connectivity, plus HDMI and DisplayPort. The VP Series consists of: This series was designed with post houses in mind and environments where professional inputs and color accuracy are paramount, but where users typically rely on a standalone scope solution and don’t need processed monitor outputs or on-monitor Look LUT support. By removing features not typically needed in post, Flanders Scientific was able to make the monitors more affordable, and they are up to 30% less than their XMP counterparts. Wth the new hardware platform, the company was able to add something the XMP series lacked: optional 3D support. Yes, it’s a niche requirement, but few professional monitoring solutions support 3D. The V Series has HDMI and DisplayPort. They are being targeted as good options for grading, editorial, VFX, etc. They are also the lowest-priced options if you want to get into FSI QD-OLED monitoring. This series was designed to complement the company’s other QD-OLED solutions for applications that don’t require professional SDI connectivity. The monitors offer the same panels and performance as their XMP counterparts at a much lower cost, up to 48% less. title: Verdict: Is the Acura ADX Just a Luxurious Honda HR-V? Yes, but That’s a Good Thing - MotorTrend
content: Acura builds a surprisingly satisfying luxury experience on a mainstream foundation. Dreams often clash with reality. Indulging in a luxury vehicle can bring style, performance, refinement, and—perhaps most important—the pride of knowing you’ve made it, that you got something better than a simple transportation appliance. At the same time, it can introduce practical perils. Think uncertain reliability, fussy interfaces, and design that compromises function for form. Over 13 months spent driving our yearlong review 2025 Acura ADX, our Acura succeeded in balancing those considerations. How it manages that balancing act will appeal greatly to some drivers and make others steer away. Here’s the rub: The ADX is just so similar to the Honda HR-V. Their dimensions, hardware, interior, features, and even paint are very alike, if not identical. Acuras always use Honda parts but typically try at least a little harder to hide those under a premium veneer. Few subcompact luxury SUV rivals share so much with a mainstream vehicle. That’s a valid concern for drivers who seek badge cachet and want their vehicle to project status in traffic. But otherwise? Not a problem, in my opinion. Honda builds practical, sensible, reliable vehicles with strong value. They tend to drive nicely, too. With that, the HR-V appeals as a normal little crossover that’s easy to use and live with. If that’s the baseline need but there’s a desire for something nicer, something more, then the ADX could be just the thing. Think of it like a luxury trim package for the HR-V, and the ADX starts to make sense. I held that frame of reference during my time with the ADX, and in that, I remained satisfied. The ADX made an adept daily driver. It’s small and easy to park, yet it’s spacious enough to fit my extra-tall self and, with the second-row seats folded, my accordingly tall custom-made bicycle without removing the wheels. It has a bunch of real buttons, which are shared with the HR-V but actuate with a nice tactile feel. In a time when fussy digital controls infest so many cars, these easy-to-use manual knobs and air vents felt like luxury in themselves. Likewise, the familiarity of unlocking with a key, pushing the starter, throwing the shifter into drive, and heading off shouldn’t be underestimated these days. This relative simplicity invites comparison to the HR-V; none of it is particularly high-tech or design-forward. Yet our high-end A-Spec model with the Advance package had touches that elevate it from its Honda basis. The off-white Orchid perforated leather with blue microsuede accents made an appealing combination, and the light upholstery resisted discoloration. The heated and ventilated front seats and heated steering wheel got plenty warm and cool. (More details in our 2025 Acura ADX interior review.) A button on the turn signal stalk activated the 360-degree camera, which became indispensable when parking and maneuvering in tight spaces. The 15-speaker Bang & Olufsen audio system sounds really good, too. For tech, the ADX borrows from the Honda parts bin. Its 10.2-inch digital gauge display looks fine and displays necessary information, but it lacks the reconfigurability and cool graphics seen in some rivals. Likewise, the 9.0-inch infotainment touchscreen had a straightforward user interface, but it’s neither as sharp nor as large as those in competitors. That said, the addition of the Google Gemini AI voice assistant midway through the loan proved to be a useful upgrade. Overall, it’s enough tech but might not impress those who equate huge screens with luxury. The ADX’s reliability and dependability upheld its maker’s reputation. It had no unexpected issues or faults whatsoever. The one scheduled service visit at about 11,000 miles included basics such as an oil change, tire rotation, and inspection of various systems. Although we paid out of pocket due to a stipulation of how Acura allocates test vehicles to media, actual Acura buyers get scheduled maintenance covered during the first 12 months or 12,000 miles of ownership. Beyond that period, owners might anticipate paying the $430.24 we did. Over the 18,652 miles we drove, the ADX averaged 25.4 mpg, reasonably close to its 27-mpg EPA combined fuel economy rating. Cost per mile came to $0.23, reasonable in the context of today’s egregious gas prices; a hybrid ADX would be a welcome addition. The closest comparison from our long-term fleet would be the 2022 Toyota Corolla Cross, another subcompact SUV, which itself underpins a luxury vehicle, the rival Lexus UX. Over its nearly 17,000-mile service life, the Corolla Cross got 29.0 mpg average at a cost per mile of $0.17. Our recently departed 2025 Acura Integra Type S also has a turbocharged I-4 engine and averaged 23.6 mpg at $0.23 per mile over 15,400 miles, not bad considering how hard we drove it. One fueling foible relates to the ADX’s gas tank size. Even though driving range is rated at 378 miles, the most we ever got from a tank was 345 miles—20 miles past the vehicle displaying zero range remaining. Oddly, the fuel gauge shows empty when there are actually two gallons left in the tank, an unnecessarily large buffer. On the plus side, the capless fuel filler is a nice convenience. Some things about the ADX irked me. Wireless Apple CarPlay connectivity was spotty; it usually connected instantly, but occasionally I’d need to select my iPhone from the touchscreen. However, after Gemini and its upgraded Google Maps capability arrived, I basically stopped using CarPlay. The passenger-side mirror tilts down in reverse but wouldn’t always rise back up to exactly where I’d set it. Most annoying was the terrible adaptive cruise control. It was extremely slow to respond to traffic ahead, sometimes taking several seconds to detect a braking vehicle. I’d see taillights illuminate then count to three or four before it reacted abruptly. This feature works better in every other Acura and Honda I’ve tried, making its application in our ADX seem like an unfortunate fluke. Whenever I drove myself, though, I enjoyed the ADX’s connected dynamics. Its 190-hp, 179 lb-ft 1.5-liter turbocharged I-4 and CVT automatic produced an objectively slow-for-its-segment 8.9-second 0–60-mph time, and wide-open acceleration was accompanied by a coarse soundtrack. But that was rarely needed. Torque arrives promptly, making the little engine feel stronger than its numbers suggest. The CVT was free of the rubber-band sensations other transmissions of this type can display, and its paddle shifters helped sharpen response in traffic or before a merge, providing a surprising degree of control. Direct, hefty steering and a firm, responsive brake pedal contributed to the almost sporty feel. Suspension tuning nicely balanced poise in corners and long-distance comfort. Road noise was fairly pervasive, though, detracting from the luxury credentials. Maybe that’s acceptable given the price. At under $46,000 fully loaded, the ADX tops out near where some rivals begin. Equipped to match the ADX, they easily cost thousands more. That makes the ADX a value play in the segment. Then again, it’s largely a luxed-up Honda HR-V with a stronger engine. It’s still somewhat loud, unsophisticated, and not especially distinctive. Even if you see panache in the Acura badge, accepting those similarities could be a reach. But as other upmarket automakers stuff their entry-level SUVs with dazzling doodads, annoying add-ons, and poseurish performance packages, the ADX takes a more predictable direction. That could appeal if you want to avoid the potential complications that come from owning an SUV from Acura’s competitors. The ADX isn’t dramatically better than an HR-V. Rather, it makes its case by being nicer in little ways. Here, any concern around the Honda connection comes down to perspective. It’s either too close to what everyone else drives or a strong basis for easy ownership. During my time with the ADX, I drove vehicles that put more emphasis on cutting-edge design, driver involvement, or absolute refinement. But returning to the ADX was always refreshing. Even if it never wowed me, it also never made me think twice about getting where I needed to go or doing what I needed to do. It just worked. And the extra layer of Acura polish smoothed out the daily grind. Is that the stuff of dreams? Perhaps not. That’s fine—the Acura ADX is built for reality.
